questions.q: What is MySQL's sql_mode system variable primarily responsible for?
options: Controlling how strictly the server validates and enforces data and SQL rules
Setting the server's default character set
Choosing which storage engine new tables use
Controlling network encryption between client and server
questions.explain: sql_mode genuinely changes server behavior around data validation and SQL syntax strictness, not just a cosmetic setting.

questions.q: Without STRICT_TRANS_TABLES or STRICT_ALL_TABLES enabled, what historically happens when you insert a string too long for its column?
options: MySQL silently truncates the value and issues a warning instead of an error
MySQL always rejects the insert with a hard error, same as SQL Server
MySQL automatically widens the column to fit the value
The insert is queued until the column is manually resized
questions.explain: This is the core behavior difference strict mode fixes — without it, bad data can get through silently instead of being rejected.

questions.q: What does ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY enforce, and why is it notable for a T-SQL developer?
options: The same rule T-SQL has always enforced: every non-aggregated SELECT column must be in GROUP BY
That every GROUP BY must include at least five columns
That GROUP BY cannot be combined with aggregate functions
That all grouped queries must also use ORDER BY
questions.explain: ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY (default since MySQL 5.7) brings MySQL in line with a rule T-SQL, Oracle, and PostgreSQL have always required.

questions.q: Why can the exact same SQL text behave differently on two separate MySQL servers?
options: Because sql_mode is configurable globally, per-session, or per-connection, and changes real validation behavior
Because MySQL randomly varies its enforcement between restarts
Because MySQL versions cannot run the same SQL syntax at all
Because sql_mode only affects SELECT statements, never INSERT or UPDATE
questions.explain: There's no single universal 'MySQL behavior' — only behavior under that server's current sql_mode setting.

questions.q: How do you check the current session's SQL mode?
options: SELECT @@sql_mode;
SHOW DATABASES;
DESCRIBE sql_mode;
EXPLAIN sql_mode;
questions.explain: SELECT @@sql_mode; (or @@GLOBAL.sql_mode for the server-wide default) is the standard way to inspect it.
